question: A 42-year-old patient schedules an urgent-care video visit 2 hours after inverting the right ankle while stepping off a curb. They can show moderate lateral ankle swelling and point with one finger to tenderness just posterior to the distal fibula. They took four steps immediately after the injury but now cannot bear weight for four steps on camera. No numbness, open wound, or gross deformity is visible. Which disposition best applies using the Ottawa Ankle Rules adapted for telehealth?
options: Treat as a low-grade sprain with home RICE only because the patient initially walked after the injury
Recommend urgent in-person evaluation and ankle radiographs because malleolar-zone pain plus posterior distal fibular tenderness and inability to bear weight meet Ottawa criteria
Prescribe an oral corticosteroid burst and arrange routine primary care follow-up in 2 weeks
Order no imaging unless bruising appears, because swelling alone is not an indication for ankle radiographs
explanation:
PATHOPHYSIOLOGY: Inversion injuries commonly stress the anterior talofibular and calcaneofibular ligaments, but the same mechanism can produce distal fibular, talar, or fifth metatarsal fractures. Pain location and load tolerance help separate uncomplicated ligament injury from clinically important fracture risk.

CLINICAL MANIFESTATIONS: A telehealth exam should establish mechanism, immediate and current weight-bearing ability, visible deformity, neurovascular symptoms, skin integrity, swelling pattern, ecchymosis, and exact self-palpated tenderness. This patient has pain in the malleolar zone, focal tenderness along the posterior edge/tip region of the lateral malleolus, and inability to take four steps during the visit. Ask the patient to compare capillary refill, toe motion, and sensation with the unaffected side because vascular or neurologic compromise supersedes decision rules.

DIAGNOSTIC APPROACH: The Ottawa Ankle Rules indicate ankle radiographs for malleolar-zone pain plus either bony tenderness at the posterior edge or tip of the lateral malleolus, bony tenderness at the posterior edge or tip of the medial malleolus, or inability to bear weight for four steps both immediately and in the clinical setting. In telehealth, the clinician can coach the patient to palpate the posterior distal fibula and medial malleolus and attempt four safe steps only if there is no deformity or severe instability. Initial ability to walk does not negate current inability in the clinical setting. If midfoot pain is present, also screen navicular and base-of-fifth-metatarsal tenderness because those Ottawa Foot Rule findings warrant foot radiographs.

MANAGEMENT: This patient should be referred for urgent in-person assessment and radiography, with interim protection, ice, compression if tolerated, elevation, analgesia, and avoidance of weight bearing until evaluated. Emergency referral is needed for open injury, gross deformity, compromised perfusion, progressive neurologic symptoms, or uncontrolled pain. Document the specific coached maneuvers and why the patient could or could not perform them safely.

KEY POINTS: Ottawa criteria are designed to reduce unnecessary imaging while maintaining high sensitivity for clinically significant fractures. Telehealth use depends on careful coaching and a low threshold for in-person evaluation when exam reliability or safety is limited.
bulletExplanation: Ottawa Ankle Rules: malleolar-zone pain plus posterior malleolar bony tenderness or inability to bear weight warrants X-ray.
Current inability to take four steps on video is clinically meaningful even if the patient walked immediately after injury.
Conservative sprain care is appropriate only when fracture red flags and Ottawa imaging criteria are absent.
Visible deformity, neurovascular compromise, open injury, or unsafe ambulation requires emergency in-person care.

question: A 56-year-old warehouse worker reports 3 days of acute low back pain after lifting boxes. Pain is across the lumbar area and radiates mildly into the right buttock but not below the knee. On video, they can heel-walk, toe-walk, squat with pain, and report normal urination. They deny saddle anesthesia, bowel incontinence, fever, cancer history, injection drug use, trauma, chronic steroid use, and progressive weakness. Which telehealth plan is most appropriate?
options: Same-day emergency department referral for MRI because any acute low back pain with buttock radiation may be cauda equina syndrome
Conservative management with activity advice, nonopioid analgesia if safe, return precautions, and follow-up because no cauda equina or serious spinal red flags are present
Immediate lumbar radiographs because nonspecific low back pain lasting more than 48 hours requires imaging
Strict bed rest for 7 days followed by referral for spinal manipulation
explanation:
PATHOPHYSIOLOGY: Most acute low back pain in urgent care is mechanical and nonspecific, arising from paraspinal muscle strain, ligamentous irritation, facet or disc-related pain without dangerous neural compression. Cauda equina syndrome results from compression of sacral and lumbar nerve roots, threatening bladder, bowel, sexual, and lower-extremity neurologic function. Disc herniation can cause radiculopathy, but radicular pain alone is different from a compressive emergency when strength and sphincter function are preserved.

CLINICAL MANIFESTATIONS: Telehealth assessment should identify pain distribution, trauma, infection risk, malignancy risk, osteoporosis or steroid exposure, anticoagulation, systemic symptoms, and neurologic deficits. Functional screening can include gait, sit-to-stand, heel and toe walking, squat or single-leg stance if safe, and patient-reported sensory changes. Cauda equina red flags include new urinary retention or overflow incontinence, fecal incontinence, saddle anesthesia, bilateral sciatica, severe or progressive motor weakness, and major neurologic deficits. Ask directly about urinary retention rather than only incontinence because retention is often the earlier warning symptom.

DIAGNOSTIC APPROACH: In the absence of red flags, routine imaging during the first several weeks of acute low back pain does not improve outcomes and may lead to incidental findings. Mild buttock radiation without objective weakness, bladder/bowel dysfunction, fever, trauma, or cancer history does not by itself mandate emergency imaging. Telehealth limitations require clear safety-netting and a lower threshold for in-person evaluation if neurologic testing is unreliable or symptoms evolve.

MANAGEMENT: Recommended care includes staying active as tolerated, avoiding prolonged bed rest, heat, ergonomic modification, gentle mobility, and NSAIDs or acetaminophen when not contraindicated. Muscle relaxants may be considered selectively for short-term severe spasm, with counseling about sedation. Arrange follow-up if not improving, and urgent evaluation for new urinary retention, saddle numbness, progressive weakness, fever, unexplained weight loss, major trauma, or severe unremitting night pain. Opioids and routine systemic steroids are generally not first-line for uncomplicated nonspecific low back pain.

KEY POINTS: The central telehealth task is not to label a precise pain generator but to distinguish uncomplicated mechanical low back pain from neurologic, infectious, malignant, or traumatic emergencies.
bulletExplanation: No bladder/bowel dysfunction, saddle anesthesia, progressive motor deficit, fever, cancer history, or significant trauma is reported.
Heel walking, toe walking, and squat are useful video-based functional screens for motor involvement.
Early routine imaging is not indicated for uncomplicated acute nonspecific low back pain.
Patients need explicit cauda equina and spinal infection/malignancy return precautions.

question: A 31-year-old patient has neck stiffness after sleeping awkwardly and working long hours at a laptop. They are afebrile, alert, and can rotate the neck about 60 degrees each way, though with trapezius discomfort. They deny severe sudden headache, photophobia, rash, immunosuppression, trauma, limb weakness, gait change, bowel/bladder symptoms, and IV drug use. Which additional finding would most strongly change the telehealth disposition from conservative care to emergency evaluation?
options: Pain worsens when they look down at a phone
Localized trapezius tenderness reproduced by self-palpation
Fever with severe headache, photophobia, confusion, or nonblanching rash
Mild stiffness that improves after a warm shower
explanation:
PATHOPHYSIOLOGY: Benign mechanical neck pain often reflects muscle strain, facet irritation, postural overload, or mild cervical disc irritation. Dangerous causes include meningitis from infection of the meninges, epidural abscess with spinal cord or root compression, fracture or instability after trauma, cervical myelopathy, and vascular emergencies such as arterial dissection. The same symptom label, neck stiffness, therefore spans disorders from self-limited myofascial pain to time-sensitive infection or cord compromise.

CLINICAL MANIFESTATIONS: Mechanical neck pain is usually localized or referred to the trapezius or periscapular region, varies with posture and movement, and lacks systemic illness or objective neurologic deficits. Telehealth exam can assess alertness, speech, fever history, rash visibility, active range of motion, shoulder shrug, arm elevation, grip symmetry using household objects, gait, and self-palpation. Red flags include fever, severe headache, photophobia, altered mental status, petechial or nonblanching rash, immunosuppression, injection drug use, recent bacteremia or procedure, significant trauma, midline bony tenderness, progressive neurologic deficit, gait disturbance, bowel/bladder dysfunction, or sudden severe neck pain with neurologic symptoms. Inability to flex the neck is less specific than the overall toxic or neurologic picture.

DIAGNOSTIC APPROACH: Fever plus severe headache, photophobia, confusion, or nonblanching rash raises concern for meningitis or meningococcemia and is not a video-manageable complaint. Cervical epidural abscess may present with neck/back pain and fever, later neurologic deficits; risk factors increase suspicion. Mechanical features such as posture-related worsening, reproducible muscle tenderness, and improvement with heat support outpatient care only after emergency features are excluded.

MANAGEMENT: For low-risk mechanical neck pain, management includes relative activity, posture changes, heat or ice, gentle range-of-motion exercises, NSAIDs or acetaminophen when safe, and short interval follow-up. Avoid high-velocity manipulation when diagnosis is uncertain. Emergency referral is appropriate for suspected meningitis, spinal cord compression, fracture/instability, epidural abscess, or vascular event. Give precise instructions to seek urgent care if fever, weakness, numbness, gait difficulty, confusion, or severe headache appears.

KEY POINTS: Neck stiffness is not synonymous with meningitis, but systemic toxicity, severe headache/photophobia, confusion, rash, trauma, and neurologic deficits should override a conservative telehealth plan.
bulletExplanation: Fever plus severe headache, photophobia, confusion, or nonblanching rash is concerning for meningitis/meningococcemia.
Video ROM and self-palpation can support mechanical neck pain when systemic and neurologic red flags are absent.
Screen for trauma, immunosuppression, injection drug use, gait changes, limb weakness, and bowel/bladder symptoms.
Conservative care is reasonable for low-risk mechanical presentations with clear safety-net instructions.

question: A 64-year-old man with known gout and normal kidney function has abrupt severe pain, redness, and swelling of the first metatarsophalangeal joint starting overnight after a seafood-heavy meal. He is afebrile, can gently move the toe, has had identical podagra twice before, and has no wound, prosthetic joint, immunosuppression, or recent injection. Which feature would most strongly require urgent in-person evaluation for possible septic arthritis rather than routine remote gout-flare management?
options: Prior similar attacks involving the same first metatarsophalangeal joint
Rapid onset of pain peaking within 24 hours
Inability to tolerate any passive joint motion, fever, systemic toxicity, or a new high-risk monoarthritis
Recent intake of seafood or alcohol
explanation:
PATHOPHYSIOLOGY: Gout flares occur when monosodium urate crystals trigger intense neutrophilic inflammation in and around a joint. Septic arthritis is infection within the joint space, most often bacterial, causing rapid cartilage destruction and systemic risk if drainage and antibiotics are delayed. Crystal arthritis and infection can coexist, so high-risk features matter even in patients with known gout. The inflammatory intensity of gout can mimic infection, which is why pattern recognition must be paired with risk assessment.

CLINICAL MANIFESTATIONS: Classic gout presents with abrupt severe monoarticular pain, erythema, warmth, swelling, and marked tenderness, often peaking within 24 hours. Podagra involving the first metatarsophalangeal joint and prior identical attacks increase diagnostic confidence. Telehealth assessment should document fever, systemic symptoms, skin breaks or cellulitis, recent joint injection or surgery, prosthetic joint, immunosuppression, diabetes severity, bacteremia risk, inability to bear weight, and whether any active or passive motion is intolerable. Ask the patient to show the skin, compare adjacent joints, and identify whether redness is spreading beyond the joint.

DIAGNOSTIC APPROACH: A typical recurrent podagra flare in a stable patient can often be treated remotely if septic arthritis risk is low. However, fever, rigors, toxic appearance, rapidly progressive cellulitis, an atypical joint, first-ever severe monoarthritis, prosthetic joint involvement, immunocompromise, recent procedure, penetrating wound, or inability to tolerate even minimal passive motion should prompt urgent in-person evaluation and often arthrocentesis. Serum uric acid is not reliable for confirming or excluding an acute flare during symptoms. Joint aspiration remains the diagnostic standard when infection is plausible.

MANAGEMENT: Remote gout treatment may include NSAIDs, colchicine, or oral corticosteroids depending on renal function, drug interactions, anticoagulation, diabetes, gastrointestinal bleeding risk, and cardiovascular history. Continue established urate-lowering therapy during a flare; do not start or adjust long-term urate-lowering therapy casually in an acute telehealth visit without follow-up planning. Provide hydration, rest, ice, and urgent precautions for fever, spreading redness, worsening pain despite therapy, or systemic illness.

KEY POINTS: Known gout lowers but does not eliminate the risk of septic arthritis. The telehealth decision hinges on whether the presentation is typical and low risk versus potentially infected and needing aspiration.
bulletExplanation: Septic arthritis red flags include fever, systemic toxicity, prosthetic joint, immunosuppression, wound/procedure, and severe pain with passive motion.
Typical recurrent podagra can often be managed remotely when infection risk is low.
Serum uric acid can be normal during an acute flare and is not a definitive urgent-care test.
NSAIDs, colchicine, or corticosteroids should be selected based on contraindications and comorbidities.

question: A 24-year-old recreational soccer player twisted the left ankle yesterday. On video, swelling is mild to moderate over the lateral ligaments, there is no deformity, no medial or posterior malleolar bony tenderness by coached self-palpation, no base-of-fifth-metatarsal or navicular tenderness, intact sensation, and they can take more than four steps with a limp. They report pain with inversion but can actively dorsiflex and plantarflex. What is the best initial telehealth management?
options: Conservative care for likely grade I-II lateral ankle sprain with protection, ice/compression/elevation, early pain-limited range of motion, progressive weight bearing, and follow-up precautions
Immediate non-weight-bearing casting for 6 weeks because all ankle sprains require immobilization
Urgent radiographs because any swelling after inversion injury meets Ottawa Ankle Rules
High-dose antibiotics and emergency referral because swelling indicates occult septic arthritis
explanation:
PATHOPHYSIOLOGY: Most inversion ankle sprains injure the lateral ligament complex, especially the anterior talofibular ligament. Grade I sprains involve microscopic stretching with minimal instability; grade II sprains are partial tears with swelling, pain, and some functional limitation; grade III injuries are complete tears with substantial instability and inability to bear weight. Fracture concern rises with bony tenderness, deformity, high-energy trauma, or inability to bear weight. Syndesmotic sprains involve the distal tibiofibular ligaments and may follow external rotation or dorsiflexion mechanisms.

CLINICAL MANIFESTATIONS: Telehealth evaluation should compare both ankles if possible, inspect swelling and bruising, coach self-palpation of the posterior medial and lateral malleoli, navicular, and base of the fifth metatarsal, assess active range of motion, ask about a pop, instability, numbness, wounds, and test safe weight bearing. This case lacks Ottawa Ankle Rule imaging triggers: the patient can take more than four steps and has no relevant bony tenderness. Functional status is often more useful remotely than attempting special tests that require clinician force.

DIAGNOSTIC APPROACH: Sprain grading is primarily functional. Mild to moderate swelling with preserved active motion and some weight bearing suggests grade I-II sprain. Grade III sprain, syndesmotic injury, tendon rupture, or fracture should be suspected when there is marked instability, severe swelling/ecchymosis, pain above the ankle mortise, inability to bear weight, deformity, neurovascular symptoms, or focal bony tenderness. Telehealth cannot perform stress testing reliably, so worsening function or uncertain findings should prompt in-person evaluation.

MANAGEMENT: Initial care is functional, not prolonged immobilization for most low-risk sprains. Use protection from reinjury, relative rest, ice, compression, elevation, and NSAIDs or acetaminophen if safe. Encourage early pain-limited range of motion, then progressive weight bearing, balance/proprioception work, and strengthening. Bracing or taping can help during recovery and return to sport. Reassessment is needed if pain or weight bearing fails to improve over several days, symptoms worsen, or red flags develop. Return to sport should wait until pain-free walking, near-normal range of motion, and sport-specific balance or hopping are restored.

KEY POINTS: Low-risk sprains are managed by functional rehabilitation. Imaging is driven by Ottawa criteria and clinical concern, not swelling alone.
bulletExplanation: Ability to take four steps and absence of malleolar, navicular, or fifth-metatarsal bony tenderness argue against immediate X-ray.
Grade I-II sprains usually benefit from early protected motion and progressive loading.
Prolonged immobilization is not routine for uncomplicated low-grade sprains.
Escalate for deformity, neurovascular symptoms, inability to bear weight, marked instability, or worsening pain.

question: A 47-year-old tennis player reports 6 weeks of lateral elbow pain aggravated by gripping a racquet and lifting a coffee mug. There was no fall or direct trauma. On video, they have full elbow range of motion, no visible swelling or redness, and reproduce pain by palpating just distal to the lateral epicondyle and by resisted wrist extension using the other hand. No numbness, weakness, fever, or neck pain is reported. What is the most appropriate telehealth plan?
options: Diagnose likely lateral epicondylitis/tendinopathy and recommend load modification, counterforce strap or wrist splint as needed, topical/oral analgesia if safe, progressive eccentric-concentric strengthening, and follow-up
Send to the emergency department for elbow radiographs because overuse pain lasting more than 2 weeks is presumed fracture
Prescribe empiric antibiotics for occult septic bursitis despite lack of swelling, warmth, or systemic symptoms
Advise complete rest of the arm for 3 months with no exercise because tendons heal best without loading
explanation:
PATHOPHYSIOLOGY: Lateral epicondylitis is better understood as lateral elbow tendinopathy, usually involving degenerative and failed-healing changes of the common extensor tendon, especially the extensor carpi radialis brevis. It is driven by repetitive gripping, wrist extension, and load spikes rather than acute infection or fracture in most cases. Tendon pain commonly reflects impaired load tolerance, so complete unloading can perpetuate weakness while excessive loading maintains symptoms.

CLINICAL MANIFESTATIONS: Patients report lateral elbow pain with gripping, lifting, racquet sports, tools, typing, or resisted wrist extension. Telehealth can assess active elbow range of motion, visible swelling or erythema, location of maximal tenderness, resisted wrist extension or middle-finger extension, grip-related pain, cervical symptoms, and distal numbness or weakness. Full range of motion, absence of trauma, and reproduction of pain at the lateral epicondyle with resisted wrist extension fit tendinopathy. Ask about occupational tool use and recent training changes because modifiable load spikes are common drivers.

DIAGNOSTIC APPROACH: Imaging is not required initially for classic atraumatic tendinopathy. In-person evaluation is appropriate for acute traumatic onset, deformity, major loss of motion, significant swelling/warmth, fever, suspected septic bursitis or arthritis, progressive neurologic deficit, severe night pain, or failure of a structured rehab program. Differential diagnoses include radial tunnel syndrome, cervical radiculopathy, osteoarthritis, inflammatory arthritis, and occult fracture after trauma. Numbness in a nerve distribution or pain reproduced by neck movement should broaden the differential.

MANAGEMENT: Treatment centers on education and graded loading. Temporarily reduce provocative gripping and wrist-extension loads while maintaining general activity. Use ice or heat, topical NSAIDs, oral NSAIDs or acetaminophen when safe, and consider a counterforce brace or wrist splint for short-term symptom control. Begin progressive isometric, eccentric, and concentric wrist extensor strengthening as pain allows, plus shoulder/scapular conditioning and technique or ergonomic changes. Corticosteroid injections may provide short-term relief but can worsen longer-term outcomes; they are not a routine telehealth first step. Arrange follow-up if no improvement over 6-12 weeks.

KEY POINTS: Overuse tendinopathy is managed with load modification and progressive rehabilitation, not antibiotics, emergency imaging, or prolonged complete rest.
bulletExplanation: Pain just distal to the lateral epicondyle with resisted wrist extension is typical for lateral elbow tendinopathy.
Initial imaging is unnecessary without trauma, deformity, swelling, fever, neurologic deficit, or major ROM loss.
Relative load reduction plus progressive strengthening is preferred over complete rest.
Red flags include fever, warmth/swelling, acute injury, progressive weakness/numbness, and persistent failure to improve.

question: A 58-year-old patient has acute right knee pain after slipping on wet stairs and twisting the knee. During the video visit, the knee appears swollen, and the patient reports focal tenderness over the fibular head. They can limp only two steps before stopping. They cannot flex the knee to 90 degrees because of pain. No open wound or neurovascular symptoms are reported. Which recommendation is most consistent with Ottawa Knee Rules?
options: Home care only because twisting mechanisms rarely fracture the knee
Urgent in-person evaluation with knee radiographs because age over 55, fibular head tenderness, inability to flex to 90 degrees, and inability to bear weight meet imaging criteria
No imaging unless bruising extends below the ankle
Treat as gout with colchicine because acute knee swelling after a fall is usually crystal arthritis
explanation:
PATHOPHYSIOLOGY: Knee trauma can injure ligaments, menisci, tendons, cartilage, or bone. Fractures may involve the patella, tibial plateau, proximal fibula, or distal femur, and can occur after twisting or falls, especially with age-related bone vulnerability. Effusion and inability to bear weight may reflect intra-articular injury or fracture. Proximal fibular tenderness is also important because associated peroneal nerve symptoms or syndesmotic injury can be missed without careful questioning.

CLINICAL MANIFESTATIONS: Telehealth triage should clarify mechanism, audible pop, immediate swelling, ability to bear weight, locking, deformity, neurovascular symptoms, anticoagulation, and prior knee disease. Video assessment can inspect alignment and swelling, compare both knees, assess active extension, coach palpation of the patella and fibular head, estimate flexion to 90 degrees, and observe safe steps only if no deformity or severe instability is present. This patient has multiple high-risk features. Ask specifically about foot drop, dorsal foot numbness, and color or temperature change distal to the injury.

DIAGNOSTIC APPROACH: Ottawa Knee Rules recommend knee radiographs after acute knee injury if any of the following are present: age 55 years or older, isolated patellar tenderness, tenderness at the head of the fibula, inability to flex to 90 degrees, or inability to bear weight for four steps both immediately and during evaluation. This case meets several criteria: age 58, fibular head tenderness, inability to flex to 90 degrees, and inability to take four steps. Telehealth cannot exclude tibial plateau or proximal fibular fracture when these criteria are present. Decision rules do not replace clinical judgment when deformity or vascular compromise is seen.

MANAGEMENT: The patient should be referred for urgent in-person evaluation and radiographs. Until evaluated, advise protection, avoidance of weight bearing if painful, ice, compression if comfortable, elevation, and nonopioid analgesia if safe. Emergency care is indicated for gross deformity, absent pulses, expanding swelling, suspected dislocation, open injury, compartment syndrome symptoms, or progressive neurologic deficits. If radiographs are negative but the patient cannot extend the knee, bear weight, or has mechanical locking, further in-person orthopedic or advanced imaging assessment may be needed.

KEY POINTS: Ottawa Knee Rules are highly sensitive screening criteria for fracture after acute knee injury and are well suited to structured telehealth triage when the clinician coaches palpation and function safely.
bulletExplanation: Ottawa Knee Rules include age 55 or older, fibular head tenderness, patellar tenderness, inability to flex to 90 degrees, or inability to bear weight four steps.
This patient meets multiple criteria, so radiographs are indicated.
Twisting injuries can still cause clinically important knee fractures.
Telehealth management should include interim protection and escalation for deformity or neurovascular compromise.
